title: Faster than earcut: triangulating 3.7M map polygons in 489 ms
why: If you ship a web map, swapping earcut for this ISC-licensed drop-in cut triangulation of 3.74M polygons from 557 ms to 489 ms natively and 1.4-2.1x in the browser, with the same API and triangle output.
notes: earstrip is one C++ header plus a WebAssembly/npm build that takes earcut's arguments; self-reported 14% faster than earcut.hpp 3.2.4 natively and 1.4-2.1x faster than earcut.js 3.2.4 in-browser, depending on call path (direct calls, all polygons in one call, hit the 2.1x figure in JavaScriptCore).

The engine replaced a constrained Delaunay triangulator (2.93s on 3.74M Masovian zoom-13 polygons, one M4 Pro core) with ear clipping, reaching 489ms; each optimization is a separate commit timed on the same data.

Load-bearing optimizations, in order of savings: test only reflex vertices (dents) not all points; skip convex polygons entirely; emit triangle strips (35.8M indices vs 64.5M); bucket dents along the bounding box for large polygons; a branchless counting pass (min of three determinants >= 0 means inside) before the exact dent loop.

Holes are bridged via David Eberly's method (ray from the rightmost hole vertex, bridge to the triangle's safe endpoint); polygons with >=128 rings fall back to Delaunay because bridge-finding scans the whole boundary each time (a world-map polygon with 11,675 holes takes earstrip 606ms vs Delaunay 17ms).

Grid rounding can destroy the simple-polygon precondition of Meisters' 1975 theorem; when no ear is found, earstrip drops zero-area corners and retries, then falls back to Delaunay (76 polygons in the older Masovian build); the map generator now uses GEOS snap rounding so a fresh build cuts every polygon.

Accuracy claim: on polygons ears can't cut exactly, earcut's triangles diverge from an even-odd fill on 31% of pixels on average versus earstrip's 0.15%; WASM builds match native triangle output on all 4.4M zoom-13/9 polygons.
summary: earstrip is an ISC-licensed polygon triangulator extracted from a map engine, shipped as a single C++ header and a WebAssembly/npm build with an earcut-compatible API. The author replaced a constrained Delaunay triangulator (2.93s on 3.74M Masovian Voivodeship zoom-13 polygons on one M4 Pro core) with ear clipping and rebuilt it one commit at a time, reaching 489ms native, reportedly 14% faster than earcut.hpp and 1.4-2.1x faster than earcut.js in the browser. Key wins come from testing only reflex vertices (dents), skipping convex polygons, emitting triangle strips, bucketing dents for large rings, and a branchless counting pass before the exact inside-triangle check. Holes are opened with Eberly-style bridges, and polygons with >=128 rings or that defeat ear clipping (grid rounding can break the simple-polygon assumption behind Meisters' 1975 two-ears theorem) fall back to the retained Delaunay code. The author reports earstrip's triangles diverge from an even-odd fill on 0.15% of pixels versus earcut's 31% on hard cases, and notes earcut.hpp loses most of its speed in its ear-search loop when compiled to WASM. All benchmark numbers are self-reported, with repository, polygons, and timing code published.
novelty: ear-clipping triangulator beats earcut via incremental optimization, open-sourced
audience: graphics/mapping engineers and computational geometry practitioners

title: OpenCode 2.0
why: If you run a coding agent against many MCP servers, OpenCode 2.0's "code mode" lets the model compose tool calls in a single scripted round trip instead of sequential calls, cutting latency and context bloat even with ~1,000 servers attached.
notes: Client/server split is now default: a single background process backs the TUI, web UI, and desktop app; the @opencode/client package autodiscovers the local service, and /pair or opencode pair exposes it to other hosts.

Code mode (@opencode/codemode) runs a minimal native JS interpreter that ingests MCP servers or OpenAPI endpoints as callable functions, avoiding Node VMs or QuickJS; agents can call a tool, map over results, and call another tool in one round trip. All MCP servers opt in by default.

Background execution added on two fronts: background subagents (the primary agent spawns work to another agent, optionally a different model, and keeps prompting) and async background shell commands; a hotkey moves any slow foreground task to the background.
Plugins: 80+ internal plugins now implement nearly every 2.0 feature to keep the Plugin API exercised; TUI plugins promoted from experimental to stable on OpenTUI.

@opencode/sdk ships OpenCode as a library (the same code as the CLI) for embedding in environments like Cloudflare Durable Objects, speaking the standard OpenCode server protocol, with an optional Effect-based API.

Breaking changes: 1.0 plugins do not work, the server API is completely different, and tui.json config moves to json; upgrade via opencode upgrade --major from the latest 1.x. The 'millions of daily users' and performance figures are vendor claims without methodology.
summary: OpenCode 2.0 is a major rewrite of the open-source coding agent that makes its client/server model the default: a single background process now serves the TUI, web, and desktop clients, with an autodiscovering @opencode/client package and a /pair flow to expose the service to other hosts. The headline feature is "code mode" (@opencode/codemode), a minimal native JavaScript interpreter that converts MCP servers and OpenAPI endpoints into functions the agent can script, letting it chain tool calls in one round trip rather than sequentially; all MCP servers are opted in by default to limit context bloat even with roughly a thousand servers attached. The release adds background subagents and asynchronous background shell commands so long-running work does not block the primary agent, plus a hotkey to push slow tasks to the background. The plugin system was rebuilt with 80+ internal plugins implementing most 2.0 features, and TUI plugins (built on OpenTUI) are now stable. A new @opencode/sdk exposes OpenCode as an embeddable library, for example in Durable Objects. Upgrading requires the latest 1.x and opencode upgrade --major, and carries breaking changes: 1.0 plugins are incompatible, the server API is entirely new, and tui.json config moves to json. Claims about "millions of daily users" and performance gains are self-reported and unquantified.
novelty: unified server process, JS-native "code mode" tool orchestration, background subagents
audience: engineers building or using AI coding agents/CLI tools

title: F-Zero X on Nintendo 3DS
why: A single developer steering one Claude session and 147+ subagents shipped a working, 60fps-in-3D N64 port to both 3DS consoles, and the decisive wins came from hardware instruction-cache profiling, not model cleverness: a concrete data point on where agentic coding actually pays off and where the human still has to make the call.
notes: One person directed throughout; one long-lived Claude session orchestrated 147 subagents in a 24-day phase 1 (2026-08-11 to 09-03) and many more in a 43-day phase 2 (2026-09-07 to 10-19), porting the inspectredc/fzerox decompilation (upstream untouched) plus a patch stack, on top of libultraship (untouched, plus a 13-line newlib fix for devkitARM); port/3ds was 15,039 lines at end of phase 1.

Phase 1 (New 3DS) hardware medians, self-reported, climbed 48-50 fps (08-21 first hardware run) to 59.6 fps with 53% of frames at cap (09-03) via levers including a render thread on core 2, one-frame-ahead mode, bridge-on-main, auto LOD, and memoizing each sub-display-list's classification instead of re-scanning every frame.

Old 3DS (268 MHz) had to fit a 64 MB app region: RDRAM arena halved, audio streamed rather than resident, texture uploads capped; the shipped New-3DS build died at boot on real hardware while the O3DS profile booted and raced at ~10 fps (09-29).

Hardware performance counters showed the real Old 3DS limit was instruction-cache misses, not instruction count; the native renderer was rebuilt as one small loop per race category sized to the 16 KB icache, reaching a 16.5 ms median frame time on a 2D Grand Prix race, and is the v1.0.0 default on both consoles.

Heaviest Old 3DS courses (Silence, Sand Ocean) can still trip a frame-skip safety net to a steady 30 fps mid-race; the 64DD Expansion Kit verified tick-for-tick identical and booted on Old 3DS but was deemed too slow to release there.

No ROM or disk image ships: every build reads prebaked asset archives from the SD card and requires a user-supplied disk image for the Expansion Kit; four builds shipped from one source tree (Old 3DS/2DS, New 3DS/New 2DS XL, and New 3DS with Expansion Kit). Dollar figures are estimates applying published API list prices to exact token counts.
summary: A post-mortem documents porting G-Diffuser, the F-Zero X decompilation, to the Nintendo 3DS, reaching v1.0.0 with four builds covering Old and New 3DS, with and without the 64DD Expansion Kit, all from one source tree. One person directed the work while one long-lived Claude session orchestrated 147 subagents in a 24-day first phase and many more in a 43-day second phase; the decompilation and the libultraship N64 runtime were used untouched upstream. On New 3DS the author reports a median 59.6 fps with 53% of frames at cap, reached through a core-2 render thread, ahead-mode rendering, and display-list classification memoization. The Old 3DS required halving the RDRAM arena, streaming audio, and capping texture uploads to fit a 64 MB app region; hardware performance counters then revealed instruction-cache misses, not instruction count, as the bottleneck, prompting a native renderer built as per-category loops sized to the 16 KB icache that hit a 16.5 ms median frame time on 2D races and 59-60 fps in 3D on most courses. The heaviest courses still drop to a frame-skipped 30 fps, and the Expansion Kit, though verified identical, was judged too slow to release on Old 3DS. No ROM or disk image ships; builds read prebaked SD-card asset archives, and reported dollar costs are estimates derived from token counts at list prices.
novelty: AI-agent-orchestrated N64 decomp port tuned via icache profiling
audience: retro/embedded systems engineers and AI-coding-agent tooling enthusiasts

title: Mosaic: Multi-Session Agentic Reinforcement Learning
why: If your agents already use context compaction or subagent forking, the standard single-session RL assumption no longer matches how they run, and broadcasting one reward across all sessions wastes credit assignment Mosaic claims to recover.
notes: Problem framing: most agentic RL assumes a single continuously accumulated context, but context compaction and subagent forking split a trajectory into multiple sessions, so training and inference-time execution diverge.

The authors define Multi-Session Agentic RL as a general setting allowing an arbitrary number of sessions per trajectory, and name the common fix, broadcasting one trajectory-level advantage to every session, as the baseline it beats.

Mosaic is critic-free and hierarchical: at the trajectory level it folds session-usage signals into advantage estimation; at the session level it shapes each session's advantage by its estimated marginal contribution.
Reported results use Qwen3.5-4B on BrowseComp: Mosaic beats broadcasting in both context-compaction and subagent-forking scenarios while averaging fewer sessions per trajectory.

Caveats: results are self-reported on a single benchmark and one 4B model, with no methodology, ablation detail, or baseline numbers in the abstract; session allocation is pitched as an open target rather than a solved one.
summary: Mosaic proposes Multi-Session Agentic Reinforcement Learning, a setting where a single agent trajectory spans an arbitrary number of sessions because of techniques like context compaction and subagent forking, which break the single-session assumption behind most agentic RL. The widely used approach broadcasts one trajectory-level advantage to all sessions, which cannot distinguish how much each session contributed or guide how sessions are allocated. Mosaic instead uses critic-free hierarchical optimization: trajectory-level advantage estimation incorporates session-usage signals, and each session's advantage is shaped by its estimated marginal contribution. On the BrowseComp benchmark with Qwen3.5-4B, the authors report that Mosaic outperforms the broadcasting baseline in both context-compaction and subagent-forking scenarios while using fewer sessions on average. The results are self-reported on one benchmark and one model, and the authors frame session utility and allocation as a direction for future work rather than a closed problem.
novelty: critic-free hierarchical RL for multi-session agent trajectories
audience: researchers/engineers building agentic RL training pipelines with context compaction or subagent forking

title: Livenerf: Has Opus 5.5 been nerfed yet?
why: If you argue about whether Claude got "nerfed," this is the first public day-0 baseline with pre-registered decision rules, and it already shows its own limit: it cannot tell an Opus 5-for-5.5 swap apart at 99% confidence.
notes: Scope: measures Opus 5.5 as served through Claude Code on a Max subscription via headless `claude -p`, not the raw API model. Launch-week baseline (days 1-10, from 2026-09-24) is treated as a reference point, not ground truth; the author notes 2025 quality incidents turned out to be infrastructure bugs, not deliberate downgrades.

Panel construction: 2,336 GPQA Diamond, MMLU-Pro, competition-math and AIME 2025-26 questions screened at 4 samples each; Opus 5.5 scored ~93% first-try and 97% were always-right-or-always-wrong, leaving 78 'sometimes right' questions. Measured selection bias: picked items' fresh pass rate rose from 54.7% to 62.0%, so power calculations use the fresh rates.

Sensitivity: one daily run of the full panel detects ~7.5 accuracy points per 10-day window. A validation swap of Opus 5 for Opus 5.5 was NOT distinguishable at 99% (-3.8 ± 6.3 points, -23% tokens); the instrument can't catch a same-family swap of that size in a validation's samples.

Secondary signal is output tokens per sample, the author's preferred early indicator: low effort = -62% tokens but only -8.3 ± 4.5 accuracy points; medium = -26% tokens, -4.2 ± 3.9 points. Effort is always passed explicitly, never left at default.

Pre-registered decision rule (PREREGISTRATION.md committed before any series data, timestamp public): a change counts only if the 99% interval excludes zero in two consecutive 10-day windows, the effect is >=3 points, and a control arm (claude-opus-5 on the panel's GPQA questions) doesn't show the same move. Stats are paired per-item differences with clustered SEs (Miller 2024). Nulls and improvements both published.

Rigor and caveats: CLI pinned (2.1.280) and harness hash enforced because a Claude Code update looks exactly like a model change; calls are hermetic (frozen prompt, no tools/MCP/memory, one turn); code graded by hidden sandboxed tests, no LLM judge. Audit flagged 8 likely-wrong answer keys and 30 ambiguous questions in the panel; nothing dropped, handled via pre-registered sensitivity analysis. First Results row lands after day 20 (~2026-10-24). Independent project, not affiliated with Anthropic; author discloses Claude helped write much of the repo.
summary: livenerf is an independent, append-only benchmark that tests one question: does Claude Opus 5.5 get quietly worse after launch? It measures the model as served through Claude Code on a Max subscription (via headless `claude -p`), which is the setting most "nerf" complaints describe, and distinguishes that from the raw API. Because the model can't be made deterministic, it freezes everything else: a 78-question panel of "sometimes right" items selected from 2,336 GPQA/MMLU-Pro/math questions, a pinned CLI and harness hash, pure-function graders, and raw logs kept forever. It runs the full panel once a day for 30 days plus a control arm (Opus 5), using UK AISI's Inspect framework and Anthropic's own error-bar statistics (Miller 2024), with a pre-registered decision rule requiring a >=3-point change clearing a 99% interval in two consecutive 10-day windows without a matching move in the control. Stated limits are frank: it detects ~7.5-point shifts per window but could not distinguish an Opus 5 swap at 99%, and an audit found 8 likely-wrong answer keys and 30 ambiguous questions handled by a pre-registered sensitivity analysis. Output token count per sample is the author's preferred early signal, since reduced effort shows up in tokens (-62% at low effort) before accuracy moves; the first Results row was due after day 20, around 2026-10-24.
novelty: rigorous pre-registered benchmark for post-launch model drift
audience: engineers/researchers skeptical of "model nerfing" claims who want statistical rigor

title: What Would A Serious AI Product Look Like?
why: If you ship LLM tooling, this is a concrete punch-list of verification affordances your product almost certainly lacks: per-claim checkboxes, citation UIs that put the source quote above the model's summary, and a sandbox that removes auto-approve modes by default.
notes: Core argument: every chatbot ships a fine-print disclaimer (Gemini: "AI can make mistakes, so double-check responses"; Claude and ChatGPT similar) that pushes verification onto the user while providing zero tools to do it; the author calls this liability-shifting legalese.

Proposed fix is a two-column worksheet: LLM output on the left, human verification notes plus a checkbox on the right; for coding, checking diffs before they hit tests would also save the extra compute burned running bad changes through CI.

Citation UI should be inverted: the literal regex-extracted quotation (not an LLM summary) plus source, publication date, and author front-and-center and large; AI editorializing shrunk to disclaimer-size until verified. Author reports chatbots "get bored" and drop citations partway through long lists.

Demands: no first-person language or apologies from a dev/research tool; non-natural-language task-specific UIs (e.g., a dedicated button for OWASP Top 10 scanning) over free-text plus MCP tools; strong data-provenance indicators distinguishing API/tool results from hallucinated output; user-visible context windows and reproducibility/replay controls beyond a third-party progress bar.

Sandbox section: calls agentic coding "unsafe-by-default," wants filesystem sandboxing with scoped deletion limits, per-operation repo snapshots for rollback, removal of auto mode and --dangerously-skip-permissions, batch plan approval, and execution against mock API services. Metaphor: labs have "tied a spring-loaded shotgun to a dog."

Organizational prescriptions (dated near end of 2026): shift rotations to counter vigilance decrement (cites Amazon's "millions of lost orders"), L&D budget to offset skill loss (dockworker/crane analogy), and mental-health resources for "AI psychosis" and "AI brain fry." Criticism applies equally to Ollama, more so given weaker open models. Claims about mental-health crises and incidents are asserted without linked studies in the excerpt.

title: Show HN: Corral – Kill every command your agent starts
why: If your CI or coding agent runs commands that fork daemons or hold pipes open, this tool returns a hard guarantee that nothing it spawned is still holding your ports, locks, or CPU when the run ends.
notes: Enforced mode puts the command in its own cgroup v2 group; one write to cgroup.kill stops every descendant, and the mode also applies --mem and --pids limits. Fallback mode needs no cgroup: corral becomes a child subreaper, scans /proc, and signals leftover processes through pidfds after re-checking each one so a reused pid never gets signaled.

Exit code 120 ('could not prove all processes stopped') overrides all other codes; other codes include 124 (time limit), 121 (memory), 122 (output), 125 (setup failed, command never started). The run ends when the command exits, not when output pipes close.

Self-reported benchmark over 10 fault programs (5 runs each, 2s limit): corral left zero processes alive in both modes; a naive Python runner hung with up to 192 leaked children on the fork test; uutils coreutils timeout 0.8.0 (not GNU) left one process alive in several daemon/fork cases. CE stopped the 256 MiB program at its limit in 0.12s.
Measured overhead to run /bin/true (vs 0.83/1.88ms direct): 11.33/19.47ms enforced, 6.64/10.01ms fallback (P50/P95). Test box: Hetzner 2-vCPU Skylake, Ubuntu 26.04, kernel 7.0.
Explicitly not a security sandbox: no limits on file, network, or privileges. Requires Linux 5.11+ (5.14+ for enforced mode); prebuilt binary is x86-64 glibc 2.36+. MIT licensed.

Stated limits: cannot see work started outside the tree (systemd-run, D-Bus, at); in enforced mode a process can escape by writing to cgroupfs itself; in fallback mode a setuid child cannot be signaled (exits 120); SIGKILL to corral itself only guarantees the direct child dies. No PTY and no CPU-time limit.
summary: Corral is an MIT-licensed Linux tool that runs a command under a time limit and guarantees no process the command spawned survives when it returns, verifying this before exiting or returning code 120 if it cannot prove cleanup. It targets the common failure modes of CI runners and AI coding agents: double-forked daemons that call setsid(), background processes that keep stdout/stderr open and hang the runner, and processes that ignore SIGTERM. Enforced mode uses a delegated cgroup v2 group and a single cgroup.kill write to stop all descendants, and adds --mem and --pids limits; fallback mode acts as a child subreaper, scans /proc, and signals processes only through pidfds after re-checking them to avoid acting on reused pids. A self-reported benchmark against GNU-style timeout (actually uutils coreutils 0.8.0) and a naive Python runner shows those tools leak processes on forked daemons and 200-child fork tests while corral leaves none; overhead to launch /bin/true is roughly 7–20ms P50/P95. It is explicitly not a security sandbox, requires Linux 5.11+ (5.14+ for enforced mode), and cannot track work escaping the tree via systemd-run, D-Bus, or at.
novelty: cgroup v2 kill-group + subreaper guarantees no orphaned processes survive a run
audience: engineers running AI agents or CI jobs that spawn untrusted shell commands

title: Agents don't need memory, they need documentation
why: If you bolt a vector-DB memory plugin onto your coding agent, this argues you are indexing stale transcript fragments instead of building the readable, committable project knowledge the agent actually needs.
notes: Characterizes every memory plugin as the same RAG pipeline: chunk session transcripts into snippets, embed into a vector DB, inject the top-5 by similarity on each prompt, expose a search tool as fallback. Extras like rerankers, multi-tier short/long-term memory, dedup daemons, and overnight 'dreamers' are dismissed as token-burning patches on a flawed base.

Five claimed failure modes: (1) similarity ranking tells you nothing about correctness, currency, or gaps; (2) snippets drop surrounding context, motivation, and environment; (3) recall treats a changing codebase's past as truth, so snippets about e.g. authentication go stale; (4) agents can't query what they don't know they're missing; (5) the store (described as ~10,000 embeddings in SQLite) is unauditable for staleness or wrong entries.

Proposed alternative: a structured Markdown 'brain' of specs, decisions, research, and indexes, generalizing beyond the single AGENTS.md file. The agent consults relevant docs before work and updates them after, shifting the loop from prompt->build->forget to prompt->consult->build->update.

Author's implementation is Operator Memory, open source at github.com/aerovato/operator-memory, used across the author's own projects for over a year. Explicitly no vector DBs, embeddings, summarizers, or background daemons; everything is plain Markdown you can read, commit, and share.
Opinion piece grounded in personal use, not a benchmark or study; no quantitative comparison against the memory plugins it critiques. Surfaced on Hacker News at 347 points and 211 comments.
summary: The post argues that AI coding agents don't need RAG-style memory plugins, they need documentation. It describes the common memory architecture as chunking session transcripts into snippets, storing them in a vector database, and injecting the top-5 similar snippets per prompt with a search-tool fallback, then lists five failures: similarity ranking ignores correctness and currency, snippets lose context, recall treats a changing codebase's past as truth, agents can't search for what they don't know, and the store is unauditable. As an alternative it proposes document-based memory: a structured Markdown 'brain' of specs, decisions, research, and indexes that the agent consults before work and updates afterward, changing the loop from prompt->build->forget to prompt->consult->build->update. The author built an open-source plugin, Operator Memory, that implements this with plain Markdown files and no embeddings, databases, or background daemons, and reports using it across projects for over a year. The argument is experiential rather than benchmarked, with no quantitative comparison to the plugins it criticizes. It reached 347 points and 211 comments on Hacker News.

title: Groupwise Agentic Grading and Advantage Redistribution for Code Agent RL
why: If you train code agents with GRPO and binary test rewards, every passing trajectory gets the same advantage, so the policy never learns to prefer clean, in-scope fixes; GAGAR adds a grader that reranks and reweights those passes.
notes: The problem: with executable tests giving binary rewards, GRPO assigns identical advantages to all test-passing trajectories in a rollout group, giving no signal to favor targeted implementations over ones with unnecessary or out-of-scope changes.
Mechanism: an SFT-trained agentic grader inspects all trajectories from a group placed in a shared workspace and ranks the test-passing candidates by implementation quality.

Redistribution is sum-preserving: lower-ranked passing trajectories are downweighted, then all passing advantages are rescaled proportionally to restore the group's original advantage sum, shifting credit toward higher-quality passes without changing the total.
Built on dynamic sampling that retains only groups containing both passing and failing trajectories.

Evaluated on pre-RL SFT checkpoints of MiMo-V2.6-Flash (310B total params) and MiMo-V2.6-Pro (1.02T total params); claimed results are improved code-agent performance, reduced trajectory-length growth, and more stable training.
Caveats: gains are self-reported with no public benchmark numbers, baselines, or ablations in the abstract; the grader itself is a trained model whose ranking quality is unverified here.
summary: GAGAR is a credit-redistribution framework for reinforcement learning of code agents that addresses a limitation of Group Relative Policy Optimization: when executable tests give binary rewards, GRPO assigns identical advantages to all test-passing trajectories in a group, ignoring differences in implementation quality and task adherence. Using dynamic sampling that keeps only groups with both passing and failing trajectories, GAGAR places a group's trajectories in a shared workspace where an SFT-trained agentic grader jointly inspects and ranks the passing candidates. It then downweights lower-ranked passes and rescales all passing advantages proportionally to preserve the group's original advantage sum, moving credit toward higher-quality implementations. The authors evaluate on pre-RL SFT checkpoints of MiMo-V2.6-Flash (310B total params) and MiMo-V2.6-Pro (1.02T total params), in both controlled code-only Flash experiments and large-scale mixed-task RL. Reported effects are improved code-agent performance, reduced trajectory-length growth, and more stable training; the abstract provides no benchmark numbers or methodology detail.
novelty: agentic grader reranks same-passing trajectories to redistribute GRPO advantages
audience: RL/post-training researchers building code agents

title: The State of Context Engineering
why: The fix for a misbehaving long-running agent is usually to delete context, not swap models: the author's practical warning line is ~200K tokens, and the same six-move toolbox still handles the newest "agents that drive their own harness" failures.
notes: Four long-context failure modes: poisoning (a bad fact lodges and won't clear, e.g. Gemini 2.5 playing Pokemon Red kept trying to bribe a guard with iced tea from FireRed's weights instead of the correct lemonade), distraction (long context overrides base knowledge), confusion (irrelevant facts skew answers), and clash (tools/skills/memory conflict).

Context distraction is quantified via 'Do as I Say, Not as I Do' (Camassa and Shiller): with an instruction to answer in Russian plus contradictory French examples, Gemma 3 12B obeys less than half the time after a few bad examples; Opus 4.6 resists longer but still breaks. Gemini 2.5's technical report appendix notes that past ~100K tokens the agent repeated past actions instead of planning.

Six fixes, all older than the problems and increasingly moved from model calls into the harness/code: context augmentation (RAG, skills), tool loadout (filter exposed tools; one enterprise loaded 600 skills per engineer at startup), quarantine (subagents with blank history), pruning (Claude Code/Codex strip stale tool results during compaction), offloading (store state in files/DB), and summarization (compaction). Demoed as ~16 lines of DSPy changes.

Two new failure modes from harness-trained agentic models: 'fighting the weights' (models overfit to training tools, so e.g. Claude Code's prompt repeats 'make parallel tool calls' up to seven times to override serial-trained habits; smaller models botch Playwright MCP calls on first try), and 'context inertia' (models fixate on one hypothesis and won't stop).

Context inertia reported by four parties in one week; shared fix is periodic forgetting while preserving the environment: Anthropic's Memento harness clears context every ~1.5 hours after writing a note; Microsoft Research's 'Fork-and-Flush'; UC Berkeley's 'Scaling Discovery Requires Forgetting' (Shangyin Tan) shows a performance jump at each context clear.

Framing is a talk transcript from AGNTCon tied to the author's forthcoming O'Reilly book The Context Engineering Handbook; cited agent-horizon numbers (METR-style) are GPT-5 ~3.4h, Gemini 3.1 ~6.4h, Opus 4.6 ~12h, with harness. Note the piece is dated 2026 and references unreleased/speculative models (Opus 4.6, Gemini 3.1, personal agents like Hermes), so treat model names and numbers as the author's claims, not verified benchmarks.
summary: A lightly edited AGNTCon talk transcript by David Breunig arguing that context engineering has stayed hard even as models improved, because each new capability creates new failure modes. It traces the arc from the late-2024 "RAG is dead" bet on million-token windows (Gemini 1.5, Llama 4 Scout's 10M tokens that never caught on due to inference cost) to the recognition that bigger contexts also admit more errors, cataloged as four failure modes: poisoning, distraction, confusion, and clash, illustrated with Gemini 2.5 fixating on iced tea in Pokemon and a translation-instruction experiment showing models drift toward contradictory in-context examples as context grows. Breunig presents six stable fixes (augmentation, tool loadout, quarantine, pruning, offloading, summarization) now pushed into the harness and demoed in ~16 lines of DSPy. The shift to long-horizon agentic models (cited METR-style horizons: GPT-5 3.4h, Gemini 3.1 6.4h, Opus 4.6 ~12h) introduces two newer failures: "fighting the weights" (overfitting to training tools, countered by repetitive all-caps prompt instructions) and "context inertia" (fixation), with Anthropic's Memento, Microsoft's Fork-and-Flush, and a Berkeley paper all converging on periodic context-clearing while preserving the environment. His recurring practical advice is to reset context (warning point ~200K tokens), and his 2027 prediction is that accumulated, conflicting agent memories/skills will make "strategic forgetting" the next problem. The thesis: output equals context times weights, and the engineer's job is deciding when to be deterministic (code) versus probabilistic (let the model drive).
novelty: taxonomy of long-context failure modes with concrete examples
audience: engineers building LLM agents/harnesses managing context windows

title: All you need is Wide Events, not "Metrics, Logs and Traces"
why: If you run observability on OpenTelemetry's three-pillar model, this argues the split is accidental complexity: one store of wide structured events subsumes logs, traces, and metrics and makes high-cardinality "slice and dice" debugging the default.
notes: A Wide Event is a flat JSON-like record with arbitrary named fields; the advice is to dump every field that might ever be relevant, so you can query for 'unknown unknowns' during an incident instead of pre-defining metrics.

Scuba, Meta's internal tool the author calls the thing ex-employees miss most, stores raw events and pre-aggregates nothing, so field cardinality is irrelevant; any field can be filtered or grouped at any cardinality.

Native sampling: each event carries a samplingRate field and the UI auto-upscales, so the real query is SUM(samplingRate) not COUNT(*), allowing per-event-type dynamic sampling while charts still show true counts.

The author maps OTel's pillars to wide events: traces/spans are events with TraceId/SpanId/ParentSpanId (topologically sortable to draw the trace view); structured logs are events with a log_message field; metrics are periodic state snapshots (the same thing Prometheus scraping does).

Caveats: the piece is opinion from personal Meta experience with no benchmarks, the in_app_purchases example is admitted as made-up, and the author concedes he is 'still not quite sure' Span exactly equals Wide Event. He blames OTel's 60+ term glossary for industry confusion and credits Honeycomb and Axiom as moving toward the wide-event model.

Claimed extensions beyond the three pillars: continuous profiling data stored as wide events and queried into flame graphs, plus log-template extraction (strip ID-like tokens, hash, group by hash to surface top errors), all from one store amenable to cross-correlation.
summary: An opinion essay arguing that observability's standard "metrics, logs, and traces" framing, as codified by OpenTelemetry's 60+ term glossary, creates industry-wide confusion, and that a single primitive, the Wide Event (a flat JSON-like record of arbitrary fields), subsumes all three. The author draws on Meta's internal Scuba system, which stores raw un-aggregated events so cardinality never matters and supports fast ad-hoc filter/group ("slice and dice") debugging of anomalies, illustrated by narrowing an ad-impressions drop down to a campaign type, OS, OS version, and app version combination. Scuba uses native sampling, where each event records a samplingRate and the UI transparently upscales aggregates (SUM(samplingRate) rather than COUNT(*)). The author maps traces to events with TraceId/SpanId/ParentSpanId, logs to events with a message field, and metrics to periodic state snapshots (as Prometheus scraping does), and notes extensions like profiling-to-flame-graph. The claims are experiential rather than benchmarked, with the author conceding uncertainty about whether an OTel Span exactly equals a Wide Event, and citing Honeycomb and Axiom as vendors already moving this direction.
novelty: argues wide structured events replace traces/metrics/logs split
audience: backend engineers and SREs designing observability systems

title: ThinkRail from JetBrains
why: If you run coding agents, this is a working pattern to copy: one git worktree per agent so parallel runs never touch main, plus a markdown spec graph the agent reads and maintains as persistent intent across sessions.
notes: Apache-2.0, from JetBrains InnovationHub; macOS, Windows, Linux, and WSL, installed via a curl|bash or PowerShell irm launcher that then opens a browser UI with the thinkrail command. Requires git and an authenticated pi provider.

Every workspace is a real git worktree under ~/.thinkrail/worktrees/ with its own branch and cwd; files, diffs, terminals, and chats scope to it, so several agents run in parallel on separate branches and main stays untouched until you merge.

The agent engine is 'pi', which runs in-process and owns models, skills, compaction, cost, and session state; ThinkRail is described as a thin host that owns the workspace, editor, and wire and 'never assembles prompts behind your back.'

Three-ring architecture: engine host (packages/server) runs an HTTP+WS server with an AgentSessionManager (one pi session per tab); a typed, versioned wire protocol (packages/contracts, types only); and a mobile-first React UI (apps/web) that can dial any host.

Specs are first-class: each module carries a SPEC.md with frontmatter (id, type, status, parent) forming a graph; the bundled pi-spec-graph extension gives the agent spec_* tools to search, navigate, and maintain it, rendered in a Specs tab.

UI uses the Monaco (VS Code) editor engine, live git diff, and real PTY terminals; multiple chat sessions per workspace stream concurrently with per-session model choice, live token/cost in the header, and mid-turn steering or queued follow-ups. The page is a product landing page with no benchmarks or methodology.
summary: ThinkRail is an open-source (Apache-2.0) agentic IDE from JetBrains InnovationHub that pairs a browser UI with the 'pi' coding agent running in-process. Its organizing idea is that each agent workspace is a real git worktree cut from a local repo, with its own branch and cwd, so multiple agents work in parallel without clobbering main until the user merges. A second idea is spec-first development: modules carry SPEC.md files with frontmatter that form a graph, which the agent reads and maintains through dedicated spec_* tools so intent persists across sessions. ThinkRail positions itself as a thin host, owning the workspace, Monaco-based editor, PTY terminals, live git diff, and a typed wire protocol, while pi owns models, skills, compaction, cost, and session state; the host claims it never assembles prompts itself. The suit, filed Friday and first reported by Billboard, seeks $150,000 per track, about $41m total, and claims Claude generates infringing output of near-verbatim copyrighted material despite guardrails the complaint calls ineffective and added only after Anthropic was caught. Lead attorney Richard Busch accuses Anthropic of building its business on copyright infringement at unprecedented scale. The article frames this as one of the first major suits brought by an artist's estate rather than labels or the RIAA (which previously sued via Sony, Universal, and Warner), potentially setting precedent for how AI firms may use existing catalogues. The claims are unproven allegations; no Anthropic response or court ruling is reported. The piece notes Spotify recently removed roughly 50m AI 'slop' songs from recommendations.
novelty: first artist-estate (not label) suit vs an AI lab
audience: AI policy watchers, legal/ML practitioners tracking copyright exposure

title: Doc2Harness: Benchmarking LLMs on Long-Horizon Harness Engineering of Coding Agents
why: If your agent's reliability depends on the harness as much as the model, this is the first deterministic test of whether a model can build that harness, and the best one still fails nearly half the cases.
notes: Two-stage design: Stage 1 has a build model, inside a fixed builder harness, construct a full candidate harness from an interface-only contract skeleton plus a development document; Stage 2 freezes that harness and drives it end to end with a scripted mock model, one isolated container per test case.
Scoring reads four observable channels, requests sent to the model, files on disk, process exit code, and command output; positive controls are used to rule out vacuous passes.
Scale: 19 frontier models, 3 independent builds each, 328 test cases. The paper reports GPT-6 Astra on top at a self-stated 53.05% pass rate and the weakest at 27.44%, a spread of about 26 points.
Even the strongest model fails nearly half the cases; reported failures cluster around how cross-cutting functionality gets split across modules.
The development document consolidates behavior patterns from twelve frontier agent harnesses, so the task is reconstructing known harness behavior rather than inventing it from scratch.
Claimed as the first deterministic benchmark for long-horizon harness engineering; numbers are from the paper abstract, with no external methodology audit provided here.
summary: Doc2Harness is a benchmark that evaluates how well LLM agents can engineer the harness that wraps a model on long-horizon, tool-using tasks, rather than measuring downstream task success under a fixed harness. It runs in two stages: a build model constructs a complete candidate harness in an isolated container from an interface-only contract skeleton and a development document consolidating behavior from twelve frontier harnesses; the frozen harness is then tested in separate per-case containers driven by a scripted mock model. Scoring uses four observable channels (model requests, filesystem state, process exit code, command output), with positive controls to prevent vacuous passes. Across 19 frontier models, each with three independent builds on 328 test cases, the paper reports GPT-6 Astra highest at 53.05% and the weakest at 27.44%, roughly a 26-point gap, with even the top model failing nearly half the cases. Failures reportedly cluster around splitting cross-cutting functionality across modules. The authors describe it as the first deterministic benchmark for long-horizon harness engineering; all figures are self-reported in the abstract.
novelty: first benchmark measuring agents building their own harness, not just task success
audience: engineers building/evaluating long-horizon coding agent frameworks

title: Tracing Subliminal Learning Through Pretraining
why: On-policy (soft-label) distillation, now standard in post-training pipelines, transmits a teacher's unrelated preferences more reliably and with less training than hard-label distillation, so your student model can inherit traits that never appear in the visible training data.
notes: Subliminal learning here means a student model inheriting traits unrelated to its training data; tested in hard-label distillation (training on numbers from a biased teacher) and on-policy soft-label distillation (student generates data, teacher's logits supply the signal), using Pythia, PolyPythia, and DataDecide OLMo checkpoints.
Transfer persisted across differences in weight initialization, pretraining data order, pretraining corpus, model size, and architecture.

Teaching ability and learning ability develop separately across pretraining checkpoints: some checkpoints are strong teachers but weak students and vice versa, and cross-model transfer can be strongly asymmetric when teacher/student roles are swapped.

Synthetic number sequences that match the teacher's number frequencies but have no dependence on the prompt or preceding numbers still induced substantial transfer in the hard-label setting, implicating raw token frequency rather than prompt-conditioned structure.
In top-K soft-label distillation, removing animal tokens from the loss reduced transfer but did not eliminate it in the same-model setting.

The authors report soft-label distillation produced more consistent transfer with less extensive training than hard-label; claims are self-reported from their own experiments with no external replication.
summary: This arXiv paper studies subliminal learning, where a language model distilled from another model inherits traits unrelated to the training data, across both hard-label distillation (students train on numbers from a biased teacher) and on-policy soft-label distillation (students generate data, teacher logits provide the signal). Using Pythia, PolyPythia, and DataDecide OLMo model families and multiple pretraining checkpoints, the authors report that preference transfer persists across differences in weight initialization, data order, corpus, model size, and architecture. They find that the ability to transmit a preference and the ability to acquire one develop separately across checkpoints, and that cross-model transfer can be strongly asymmetric when teacher and student roles are reversed. Probing the carrier of the signal, they show synthetic number sequences matching only the teacher's number frequencies (with no prompt or sequence dependence) still induce substantial transfer in the hard-label setting, while removing animal tokens from the loss in top-K soft-label distillation reduces but does not eliminate transfer in the same-model case. They report soft-label distillation yields more consistent transfer with less training than hard-label, framing unintended preference transfer as relevant to the growing use of on-policy distillation in post-training.
novelty: traces subliminal trait transfer across pretraining checkpoints and distillation modes
audience: ML researchers studying distillation safety and model training dynamics

title: A 10-year-old CNN outperforms frontier LLMs for skin cancer diagnosis
why: If the claim holds up, a purpose-built image classifier from a decade ago still beats general-purpose frontier LLMs on a clinical imaging task, a caution against swapping specialized diagnostic models for prompt-driven multimodal systems.
notes: Central claim: a roughly 10-year-old convolutional neural network outperforms current frontier LLMs at skin cancer diagnosis from images. No article text was available, so the dataset, model identities, metrics (sensitivity, specificity, AUC), and test protocol are unverified here.

The comparison pits a task-specific supervised CNN against general multimodal LLMs; the framing suggests specialization still wins on narrow medical imaging, but the magnitude and task definition are not confirmed from the source.
Which frontier LLMs were tested, how they were prompted, and whether they saw raw images or descriptions are not available in the provided material.
No information on sample size, class balance, or whether results are peer-reviewed versus a self-published lab write-up (hosted on lynchlab.net).
Surfaced on Hacker News at 154 points with 84 comments as of first sighting on 2026-10-25; discussion volume is a signal of interest, not of methodological rigor.
summary: A write-up hosted at lynchlab.net claims that a convolutional neural network roughly ten years old outperforms current frontier large language models at diagnosing skin cancer from medical images. It is also unclear whether the work is peer-reviewed or a self-published lab analysis. The post drew attention on Hacker News (154 points, 84 comments) on 2026-10-25. title: He Wants AI Benchmarking To Be a Science, Not a Dark Art
why: The headline vendor benchmark number (90% on a math test) tells you almost nothing about a model's absolute capability, but the rank order it produces has held up across datasets for 60 years, and that load-bearing property breaks in the LLM era because builders train on different, benchmark-tuned data mixes.
notes: Moritz Hardt (Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems) argues in his 2026 book 'The Emerging Science of Machine Learning Benchmarks' that benchmarks were 'the mistake that made machine learning' and drove progress anyway, 'mostly by sheer luck.'

His central empirical claim: absolute accuracy swings wildly with small test-set changes (e.g. 90% on one dataset, 73% on a near-identical one), yet relative rankings between models stay stable across datasets, which is what let ML avoid a replication crisis. He stresses there is no comprehensive theory for why rankings stay stable.

The stability holds only under one condition: models trained on the same training set. LLMs break it because their training data is unknown and can be assembled to favor specific benchmarks, so a worse model can win by 'benchmaxxing' (post-training on earlier benchmarks); the tell is strong scores on benchmarks released before a model and weak scores on ones released just after.

Historical framing: first benchmark in 1959 (punch-card character recognition with a train-test split); 1987 DARPA speech-to-text benchmark showed AI losing to statistical methods and helped trigger an AI winter; 2012 ImageNet win by an 8-layer net started the deep learning revolution. Hardt says ML ignored the textbook 'holdout method' by publishing test sets online, enabling leakage into development loops.

Proposed fix ('altitude training', by analogy to the 1968 Mexico City 1,500m won by a high-altitude-trained Kenyan runner): drop the training set entirely, keep a test set, and add a standardized protocol that trains every model briefly on benchmark-relevant data to level the field and restore ranking validity. Caveat he concedes: this yields progress indicators, not valid absolute measurements or mechanistic understanding; he cites CASP protein folding as proof benchmarks can advance science without a prior theory.

Model names in the piece (GPT-6 Astra, Claude Fable) appear as the article's own examples, not products tied to cited results; all performance figures are illustrative, and no vendor methodology is examined.
summary: In a Quanta interview tied to his 2026 book 'The Emerging Science of Machine Learning Benchmarks,' Moritz Hardt argues that AI benchmarking has been broken for decades but worked anyway by luck. His key distinction: a benchmark's absolute accuracy number is unreliable (small test-set changes produce large swings and should not support claims like 'equal to an expert mathematician'), but the relative ranking of models has stayed stable across datasets for roughly 60 years, which is why ML avoided a replication crisis. That stability depends on all models sharing a training set, a condition LLMs violate because their undisclosed, benchmark-optimized data mixes let worse models win via 'benchmaxxing.' Hardt proposes replacing the training set with a standardized 'altitude training' protocol that prepares each model on benchmark-relevant data before testing, restoring ranking validity even as absolute scores inflate. He concedes this still yields only progress indicators rather than mechanistic understanding, but points to CASP protein folding as evidence that benchmarks can drive scientific gains without a prior theory. He offers no formal theory for why rankings stay stable, calling it an empirical phenomenon.
novelty: rankings are stable even when absolute benchmark scores aren't
audience: ML researchers and engineers who rely on benchmark leaderboards

title: Hackers stole millions of US military personnel records during months-long data breach
why: If you ever served or worked for the DoD, your unencrypted Social Security number, birth date, and service record sat exposed for nine months, and the Pentagon's "no evidence of misuse" comes with no stated basis.
notes: Breach ran October 2025 to mid-July 2026, exploiting a vulnerability in an unspecified file-sharing system used by the Defense Manpower Data Center (DMDC); multiple unauthorized users had access.
A Pentagon official (via CNN and Federal News Network) put the scope at ~2.8M living people and close to 300,000 deceased; for context, the active-duty force was 1.3M as of March.
Exposed records were unencrypted and included SSNs, name, date of birth, sex, race, and military service details.
DMDC is the DoD's identity management provider, maintaining 60M+ records and linking personnel to smart cards, passwords, and physical/computer access to Pentagon systems, buildings, and bases.

DoD says it has no indication the data was misused but did not explain how it reached that conclusion; the attackers are unidentified, and TechCrunch got no reply on whether officials heard from them.
Follows the September 2026 FBI breach attributed to ShinyHunters and echoes the 2015 OPM breach of 22M+ records broadly attributed to China.
summary: The U.S. government is reportedly notifying millions of current and former military service members and staff that their personal data was stolen in a months-long breach of DMDC personnel records. Per a breach notice shared on Reddit, unauthorized users exploited a vulnerability in an unspecified file-sharing system between October 2025 and mid-July 2026, exposing unencrypted SSNs, names, dates of birth, sex, race, and service information. DMDC maintains over 60 million records and functions as the DoD's identity management provider, tying personnel to credentials used for access to Pentagon systems, buildings, and bases. The DoD said it has no indication the data was misused but offered no basis for that assessment, and the attackers remain unidentified. The incident follows the September 2026 ShinyHunters breach at the FBI and recalls the 2015 OPM breach of more than 22 million records attributed to China.
novelty: unencrypted PII of 3M+ military personnel exposed for 9 months
audience: security engineers and policy watchers tracking federal breach patterns

title: FLIP Fluid on Flip Dots
why: Driving salvaged flipdot panels fast enough for a fluid sim means solving a 50-amp transient problem on a per-dot budget cheaper than the one remaining vendor's $50,000 floor, and this writeup documents the full dead-end tour that got there.
notes: Each flipdot is a non-volatile bistable mechanism: two permanent magnets (one in the dot, one in the base) and two polarizable cores. A dot takes ~60ms to physically flip but only needs a pulse of roughly 1ms to set the cores; original matrix drive circuits take about one second to refresh the whole panel.

Panels are 13x28 (dots made in groups of seven give the 28; 13 is attributed to the designer liking primes), date-coded 2007, donated via Look Mum No Computer's obsolete-tech collection. Only one manufacturer (AlfaZeta) reportedly still makes these; old eBay units are mostly Hanover.

Power is the binding constraint: each coil is ~18 ohms (666mA at 12V), so flipping all dots at once approaches 50A for a millisecond; direct matrix driving would need to push/pull 13A per column. Instead the build uses cheap SOIC-8 motor-driver H-bridges (MX6208/BE6208/LK6208, 0.5A rated) in single-ended mode plus series capacitors, driven by 74595 shift registers.

The H-bridges are BJT-based, not FET: an enabled output draws ~24mA from base currents even unconnected, so leaving outputs powered to fight capacitor self-discharge was abandoned in favor of periodic re-pulsing (AIN tied to latch as an enable). Flipping high-to-low is faster because low-side switching sinks more current than the high side sources.

When the power supply sags, pulses demagnetize the cores instead of polarizing them and dots go slack. Fixes across PCB revisions: swapping tiny 0805 ceramics for 47uF caps, adding a P-channel FDN338P to boost latch drive, a 3.3V regulator, 12V sense to refuse pulses during brownout, a polyfuse, and a 100-pack of 1000uF electrolytics for bulk charge.

Author built a single-schematic-per-row hierarchical KiCad setup (with Python wrangling around the new UUID system) to avoid annotation mismatch when duplicating layouts; eight dots per shift register in single-ended mode halves register count and clocked data versus full H-bridge use.
summary: An EMF2026 installation pairs an LED fluid simulation with electromechanical flipdot displays, chosen so the dots supply the "swishing" sound the silent LED version lacks. Because new flipdots are gated behind a single manufacturer and studios quoting $50,000 minimums, the author built from salvaged 13x28 panels (date-coded 2007) donated through Look Mum No Computer. The core challenge is speed and power: dots flip in ~60ms but need only ~1ms pulses, while the original matrix drivers take about a second per update and fast simultaneous flipping approaches 50A. The adopted design solders new boards onto the backs of existing panels, using cheap BJT-based SOIC-8 motor-driver H-bridges run single-ended with series capacitors and 74595 shift registers, grounding one dot pin to avoid cutting traces. The writeup walks through rejected alternatives (desoldering all dots, gate drivers, high-voltage CMOS shift registers, discrete half-bridges) and iterative PCB revisions fixing capacitor selection, latch drive current, and supply brownout. All performance figures and cost claims are the author's own from a work-in-progress build.
novelty: fluid-sim physics driven on reverse-engineered flipdot matrix hardware
audience: hardware hackers and embedded/electronics engineers

title: Yes, no AI is now a feature
why: If you deploy LibreOffice across an org that bars cloud data egress, the default install stays AI-free and telemetry-free, and any AI you add comes as a third-party extension you must vet yourself.
notes: LibreOffice 26.8 ships with no AI feature enabled by default; the post frames this as a deliberate policy, not an oversight.

The Document Foundation lists six conditions any default-on AI must meet: user-chosen inference location (local, user-controlled infra, or independently chosen service), no content transmission without authorization, zero telemetry, no single-provider API lock-in, output in ODF with structure/styles/semantics preserved, and fully optional/installable/removable and absent from the UI for admins who disallow it.

The project states no current integration meets all six, so none will be shipped on by default or supported across a release lifecycle; it calls this an assessment of the technology, not a judgment on the AI sector's value.

AI is available today only via third-party extensions maintained by their authors, not TDF; most connect to a local model through Ollama, LM Studio, or another OpenAI-compatible endpoint so the document stays on the machine. TDF warns users to check whether a cloud endpoint is configured and what the provider does with the data.

The post attributes its stance to being a nonprofit with no subscription tiers, upsells, or data to monetize, contrasting with paid suites where an AI assistant justifies price increases and keeping documents inside vendor infrastructure.
TDF leaves the door open: it cites improving on-premises inference on standard hardware and faster-than-expected open models, and says it will evaluate any approach that meets all conditions.
summary: The Document Foundation published a post explaining why LibreOffice 26.8 ships with no AI feature enabled by default, responding to a comment asking whether "no AI" was itself a feature. It sets six conditions any default-on AI integration must satisfy: user-controlled inference location, no content leaving the computer without authorization, zero telemetry, no single-provider lock-in, ODF output preserving structure and semantics, and being fully optional and removable including for admins deploying at scale. It states that no existing integration meets all six and so none will be enabled by default, framing this as an assessment of current technology rather than a rejection of AI. Users wanting AI can install third-party extensions, most of which route to a locally running model via Ollama, LM Studio, or an OpenAI-compatible endpoint so documents stay on-device; these are maintained by their authors, not TDF, and users are told to verify endpoint and data-handling. The post attributes its divergence from commercial suites to being a nonprofit with no subscriptions or data to monetize, and says it will reevaluate if an approach meeting all conditions emerges as on-premises inference and open models improve.
novelty: nonprofit office suite publishes explicit no-default-AI criteria
audience: devs/admins weighing AI feature integration and data governance tradeoffs

title: Meta releases Muse Spark Open, a new ‘open-weight’ AI model

Positioned explicitly against the open-weight leaders Meta names as Chinese: Alibaba's Qwen, Moonshot AI's Kimi K3, and Z.ai's GLM. Meta claims it competes on a similar level and in some cases outperforms them, again without cited results.

Open-weight means the parameters (weights and biases) are downloadable and modifiable, unlike closed models such as Anthropic's Claude or OpenAI's ChatGPT. Meta describes it as "built for coding and agentic work," with strength in long-horizon tasks, complex software engineering, and multi-step reasoning.

Meta says the model is optimized for Apple's M5 Ultra and that two Mac Studios with M5 Ultra chips can run it as a desktop "supercomputer" - described as an unusual Meta-Apple partnership, though no commercial terms are given.

Launch lands days after Meta's newest closed model, which it claimed rivals the most advanced ChatGPT and Claude versions, marking a shift from Meta's open-first history toward competing on both fronts under Zuckerberg.
summary: Meta launched Muse Spark Open, an open-weight AI model its AI chief Alexandr Wang claims is the most capable US open-weight model to date, positioned against Chinese open-weight leaders Alibaba Qwen, Moonshot AI's Kimi K3, and Z.ai's GLM. Meta markets it for coding and agentic work, citing strength in long-horizon tasks, complex software engineering, and multi-step reasoning, plus unspecified \"strong safeguards.\" The model is optimized for Apple's M5 Ultra chips; Meta says two M5 Ultra Mac Studios can run it as a desktop \"supercomputer,\" an unusual nod to an Apple partnership. The release follows days after Meta's newest closed model, which it claimed rivals top ChatGPT and Claude versions, reflecting a strategic shift from Meta's earlier open-first focus toward competing with closed frontier labs. The article provides no benchmark numbers, methodology, parameter counts, or licensing details; all performance claims are Meta's own.

title: Attention people who think UB is fine
why: If you ship C or C++ and assume undefined behavior degrades gracefully to a segfault, these godbolt disassemblies show GCC 16.2 at -O1 silently running an uncalled function instead of your code.
notes: A function ending in std::unreachable() compiles under GCC 16.2 -O1 (and clang) so the next function in memory, explode(), runs in its place: device_command gets 3 instead of only 42, because the compiler drops the function's trailing ret and falls through.

Replacing std::unreachable() with a nullptr write (*ptr = 99) under GCC emits a write of 0 (not 99) to address 0 followed by a ud2 invalid-instruction trap; the value 99 never appears in the binary. The author speculates the address-0 write exists to improve debugger diagnostics.

Adding pointer arithmetic (ptr += 10, then *ptr = 99), which the author notes is UB for three separate reasons, instead produces the naive result: a write of 99 to address 40. Same class of UB, different outcome.

The author's framing: compilers are not obligated to detect UB, and by the halting problem cannot in general know whether UB-containing code executes, so structurally identical UB yields different machine code case by case.
All examples are self-reported single-case disassembly from one author on GCC 16.2 and clang via Godbolt; no methodology beyond the shown output, and behavior is compiler- and version-specific.
summary: A follow-up post rebuts the claim that undefined behavior in C/C++ is harmless or at worst a segfault, using disassembly from GCC 16.2 at -O1 and clang on Godbolt. In the first example, a function whose body ends with std::unreachable() loses its return and falls through into the next function (explode()), so code that was never called executes. Swapping in a null-pointer dereference (*ptr = 99) makes GCC emit a write of 0 to address 0 followed by a ud2 trap, with the value 99 absent from the binary. Adding pointer arithmetic (ptr += 10) before the dereference, which the author argues is UB for three independent reasons, instead yields the naively expected write of 99 to address 40. The author's point is that compilers need not detect UB and, per the halting problem, cannot in general, so the same class of UB produces arbitrary and divergent results. The evidence is single-case, author-reported output tied to specific compiler versions.
novelty: concrete godbolt examples showing UB causes arbitrary, not just segfault, behavior
audience: C/C++ engineers who dismiss UB as "fine in practice"

title: Neural chip decodes interactions between brain regions
why: Adaptive brain implants for depression and OCD have been stuck reading one region at a time; LogSync pulls cross-region synchrony biomarkers and runs the classifier on-chip under 200 microwatts, making network-level closed-loop psychiatric stimulation feasible within an implant's power budget.
notes: LogSync is a 32-channel implantable system-on-chip that extracts oscillation strength and cross-region synchrony, then runs an ML classifier to detect cognitive/emotional states and emit stimulation triggers; results published in IEEE Journal of Solid-State Circuits, Sept 2026 (a 196-microwatt earlier version appeared at 2025 VLSI Symposium).

Reported total power is under 200 microwatts, which the lead describes as a fraction of typical implantable neural-interface systems; the chip uses logarithmic computation to cheapen the operations needed for synchrony and biomarker extraction. No independent benchmark or comparison methodology is given in the article.

Validation is early: human results come from replaying prior psychiatric recordings (cognitive engagement during a mental task, emotional arousal from video clips), not a live implant; phase-locked stimulation triggering was demonstrated in rats at the University of Minnesota.

The premise, attributed to lab head Mahsa Shoaran, is that psychiatric disorders stem more from disrupted communication between brain regions than single-region dysfunction, which motivates network-level over single-region closed-loop DBS.

Funded by a CHF 6.6M US NIMH grant plus an SERI-funded ERC Starting Grant; Shoaran's EPFL Integrated Neurotechnologies Lab co-founded spin-off Infera Neuro. Separate ICML 2026 work (RECTOR) uses self-supervised learning across region/channel/time instead of predefined biomarkers.
The team positions the synchrony-trigger capability as applicable beyond psychiatry: adaptive DBS for movement disorders, closed-loop non-invasive stimulation, and focused-ultrasound interfaces.
summary: EPFL's Integrated Neurotechnologies Lab (Mahsa Shoaran) built LogSync, a low-power implantable 32-channel system-on-chip that records brain activity, extracts oscillation-strength and cross-region synchrony biomarkers, and runs an on-chip machine-learning classifier to detect cognitive and emotional states and generate stimulation triggers. It uses logarithmic computation to keep the full pipeline under 200 microwatts, which the team claims is a fraction of typical implantable neural interfaces, and is published in IEEE JSSC (Sept 2026), building on a 196-microwatt VLSI 2025 version. The work targets a gap in deep brain stimulation: most systems are open-loop or single-region closed-loop, whereas psychiatric disorders are argued to involve disrupted communication across brain networks. Validation so far is early-stage: human psychiatric states were decoded from previously recorded datasets, and phase-locked stimulation triggering was shown in rats at the University of Minnesota, not in a live human implant. It was developed under a CHF 6.6M US NIMH grant; a related ICML 2026 paper (RECTOR) explores self-supervised learning over regions, channels, and time, and Shoaran co-founded EPFL spin-off Infera Neuro.
novelty: chip decodes cross-region brain synchrony for adaptive psychiatric DBS
audience: neurotech engineers, implantable-hardware and bio-ML researchers

title: MAI-Gym: An Open All-in-One Platform for GUI Agent Evaluation and RL Training across Mobile and Computer Environments
why: If the claimed sim-to-real transfer holds, you can train GUI agents against resettable mock apps instead of flaky real devices, and the full stack plus a sub-10B checkpoint ships open for you to run.
notes: MAI-Gym unifies evaluation, data collection, and online RL for GUI agents across mobile, computer, and web through one shared rollout pipeline, so agent behavior is claimed consistent between training and eval; it supports ten established benchmarks and scales to 20,000 parallel environment instances.

MAI-Gym-9B is a unified 9B agent reported at 78.4% on MobileWorld and 76.2% on OSWorld-Verified, claimed state-of-the-art among open GUI agents under 10B parameters (self-reported, no external methodology shown in the abstract).

The headline transfer result: RL trained in a mocked train-ticketing app lifted success on the real app on a physical phone from 28.8% to 48.1%, a single-domain datapoint rather than a broad sim-to-real claim.

The platform synthesizes GUI apps and tasks automatically, including resettable mocked apps and cross-app 'worlds' with execution-validated task verifiers, addressing the stated bottlenecks of interactive-environment cost and task scarcity.

Released artifacts: the framework, synthesis skills, mocked apps, 2,000 verified tasks, and the model checkpoint; the abstract gives no baseline comparisons, compute cost, or details on the verifier reliability.
summary: MAI-Gym is an open platform that combines GUI-agent evaluation, data collection, and online reinforcement learning across mobile, computer, and web environments using a single shared rollout pipeline, supporting ten benchmarks and scaling to 20,000 parallel environment instances. To address the cost of interactive environments and scarcity of realistic tasks, it automatically synthesizes GUI apps and tasks, including resettable mocked apps and coherent cross-app worlds with execution-validated verifiers. The authors train MAI-Gym-9B, a unified 9B mobile/computer agent, and report 78.4% on MobileWorld and 76.2% on OSWorld-Verified, which they claim is state-of-the-art among open GUI agents under 10B parameters. They report that RL in a mocked train-ticketing app transferred to the real app, raising success on a physical phone from 28.8% to 48.1%. The framework, synthesis skills, mocked apps, 2,000 verified tasks, and model checkpoint are released. All benchmark numbers are self-reported in the abstract without external methodology or baseline comparisons.
novelty: unified GUI-agent RL env scaling to 20k parallel instances w/ sim-to-real transfer
audience: researchers/engineers building GUI/computer-use agents and RL training infra

title: The Economics of Open-Weight Inference
why: If your workload tolerates latency, this paper's math says a five-year-old A100 serves gpt-oss-120b at $0.29 per million output tokens versus the H100's $0.64, so the default assumption that each NVIDIA generation retires the last one does not hold for inference you control.
notes: On gpt-oss-120b (a sparse MoE with 5.1B active parameters, MXFP4 expert weights, served on a single 80GB A100), the computed A100 cost is $0.12/M output tokens at full use and $0.29 base case, below the H100's $0.27 and $0.64. The authors flag that the A100 and H100 sparse numbers come from different third-party serving setups, not matched MLPerf runs.

The ranking reverses by workload: for dense Llama-2-70B, newer hardware (B200 at $0.16 full use) wins, and the dense A100 row is explicitly estimated from a vendor throughput ratio, where different precision assumptions can flip the result.

Self-hosted compute-only cost ran $0.12-$0.35/M output tokens at full utilization; the cheapest qualifying open-weight model, standardized on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, cost roughly one fifth of a comparable closed model, but only at some score thresholds (closed models win at others, and lead at the top of the range).

Ornn's five-year A100 term mark retains 80.2% of its one-month price versus 43.7-59.8% for Hopper and 53.8% for Blackwell, for a contract ending when Ampere is 11.3 years old; these are analyst-produced forward marks, not executable quotes.

A100 occupancy rose from 74% (1 Mar 2026) to 90% (1 Sep 2026) while listed capacity grew 13% and the spot index rose 20%; the paper explicitly does not establish that open-weight demand caused this, naming device retirements, dense inference, and scarcity as alternatives.

Conflict disclosed: Ornn Data publishes the paper and the rental index, occupancy series, and term marks it uses, licenses the data commercially, and runs GPU rentals via Ornn Compute. The abstract also cites NVIDIA's acquisition of Hugging Face dated 3 September 2026.
summary: Ornn Data argues that open-weight inference demand gives older NVIDIA GPU families a multi-year earning life, countering the assumption that each new generation makes its predecessor obsolete. Using the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index across eleven open and eight closed models plus its own rental data, the paper reports that self-hosted compute-only costs run $0.12-$0.35 per million output tokens at full utilization, and that for the sparse gpt-oss-120b model the A100 serves output more cheaply than the H100 at spot and at three- and five-year terms ($0.29 vs $0.64 base case), while dense Llama-2-70B favors newer hardware. Its five-year A100 term mark retains 80.2% of the one-month price versus 43.7-59.8% for Hopper and 53.8% for Blackwell. A100 occupancy rose from 74% to 90% between March and September 2026 even as listed capacity grew 13%. The paper repeatedly cautions that forward marks are analyst indicators not executable quotes, that sparse A100/H100 figures combine different third-party setups and the dense A100 row is estimated, and that it does not establish open-weight demand as the cause of the rental behavior. Ornn discloses a commercial interest: it sells the underlying data and offers GPU rentals.
novelty: older GPUs retain value via open-weight inference demand, with rental market data
audience: infra/ML economics people deciding GPU depreciation, buy-vs-rent, and open vs closed model deployment

title: Forced to pick, Grok’s AI model chooses Republicans. OpenAI’s picks Democrats.
why: The same frontier models that refuse political questions in their consumer apps will name a partisan pick through the API that developers embed in products, and this study shows the two leading models disagree on who to vote for in over 90% of races.
notes: Forced-choice prompt via API across ~500 2026 midterm races: Grok 4.7 picked the Republican in 92% of answers, GPT-6.1 Sol picked the Democrat in 97%, and the two agreed less than 10% of the time. In deep-red districts GPT still picked the Democrat in 57 of 67; in deep-blue districts Grok picked the Republican in 47 of 72.

The mechanisms differ: with internet search disabled on a 30-race sample, GPT's Democratic lean held (24/30 Democrat, 1 Republican, 5 declined), so Parikh says it is 'in the weights'; Grok's lean vanished (refused 27/30, picked Democrat the other 3), so its bias is driven by search terms and sources, not weights.

Sourcing split by party: Grok surfaced a Christian conservative voter guide in 39% of answers, Turning Point Action in 23%, and X in 41%, alongside nonpartisan Ballotpedia/OpenSecrets/VoteSmart; GPT leaned on Wikipedia, AP, Axios, and Reddit, with AP/Axios/Reddit all being OpenAI content-deal partners.

Every Grok API request carried ~1,240 tokens of input the researchers did not write and could not see or remove; Parikh calls these possible 'hidden instructions' and believes they do not come from the weights, but their contents are unverified.

Study by Convovo, led by Cornell professor Tapan Parikh, released under two weeks before the November 3 midterms. Consumer apps refused the direct prompt but Parikh says he jailbroke them with simple prompts; OpenAI's spokesperson says the API with a prompt demanding a pick does not reflect normal ChatGPT use. xAI (labeled SpaceXAI in the article) did not comment in time.

Context offered as claims, not proven cause: Pew says only 8% of Americans use chatbots for election info; Musk has donated upwards of $445M to GOP midterm candidates; Altman says he isn't funding the 2026 races. Parikh suspects both models hunt for justifications of pre-existing leans, and Grok flipped to the Democrat when the Republican faced controversy.
summary: A Convovo study led by Cornell's Tapan Parikh prompted Grok 4.7 and GPT-6.1 Sol via API to name one candidate without hedging across roughly 500 2026 midterm races; Grok picked the Republican 92% of the time and GPT picked the Democrat 97%, agreeing in under 10% of races, with the leans holding even in districts dominated by the opposite party. Consumer apps refused the question, which OpenAI stressed reflects normal use, though Parikh says simple jailbreaks reproduced the leans. Disabling internet search on a 30-race sample isolated the cause: GPT's Democratic lean persisted (bias in the weights) while Grok's Republican lean disappeared and it mostly refused (bias driven by its search terms and sources). Sourcing diverged by party, with Grok surfacing a Christian conservative voter guide (39%), Turning Point Action (23%), and X (41%), and GPT leaning on Wikipedia, AP, Axios, and Reddit, the latter three OpenAI content partners. The researchers also found every Grok API request carried ~1,240 tokens of unseen, unremovable input Parikh suspects are undisclosed instructions, though their contents remain unverified. OpenAI disputed the framing; xAI did not comment.
novelty: API-level forced-choice study exposes divergent partisan leans and hidden tokens
audience: AI policy watchers, engineers building on LLM APIs, political tech researchers

title: Elon Musk Just Gave Europe a Reason to Replace American Technology
why: If you sell software into European defense or government, "who holds the kill switch" is now a procurement question you answer before the first meeting, and sovereignty just became a sellable feature for your European competitors.

summary: Steve Blank argues that a reported decision by Elon Musk to personally restrict US intelligence sharing and Starshield (the military Starlink) access to Ukraine, which he says tilted the war toward Russia, has convinced European policymakers that the US is an unreliable technology and security partner. He projects tens to hundreds of billions in lost revenue for US vendors over time. The claims about Musk's decision and its battlefield effect rest on cited reporting; the revenue estimate is the author's own projection without stated methodology.
