title: Persistent Databases in the Browser with DuckDB-Wasm and OPFS
why: A local-first browser app can now keep analytical data across sessions by opening a real .duckdb file in OPFS, dropping the IndexedDB-plus-Parquet-serialization layer that persistence used to require.
notes: Opening `db.open({path: 'opfs://analytics.duckdb', accessMode: READ_WRITE})` yields a standard .duckdb file with a WAL and checkpoints that survives reloads and browser restarts; the file opens unchanged in the CLI or Python client. Relies on OPFS, in major browsers since March 2023.

Version caveat: the npm `latest` tag (1.33.1-dev57.0) creates OPFS files but never writes to them because it canonicalizes the path to single-slash `opfs:/analytics.duckdb`, which stops matching the OPFS handle. Pin 1.32.0 or use `next` (1.33.1-dev64.0+).

A browser tab rarely closes cleanly, so run `CHECKPOINT` after each batch of writes, not per statement: committed transactions sit in the WAL until a checkpoint flushes them to the main file, and a large WAL slows the next open because replay runs before the first query. Default checkpoint_threshold is 16 MB; `SET checkpoint_threshold = '0KB'` forces a checkpoint per statement at a write-throughput cost.

`CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS ... AS SELECT FROM 'https://...parquet'` fetches the remote file via HTTP range requests only on first load; later loads serve from OPFS with no network request, verifiable via the Network tab or the ConsoleLogger's HTTP-read log lines.

`opfs: {fileHandling: 'auto'}` scans each statement for single-quoted `opfs://` literals and registers them (creating missing directories) before execution; it only works when the database itself was opened from an opfs:// path. Manual mode avoids re-acquiring an access handle per statement. One handle per file at a time, so dropFile() before another connection opens it.

OPFS is not durable: the browser can evict it under disk pressure or after long disuse, and users can clear it. The post recommends keeping the source of truth elsewhere (DuckLake catalog or s3:// object storage) and treating OPFS as a fast local cache; DuckDB-Wasm cannot yet move files into or out of OPFS, so export goes through the navigator.storage file API or COPY TO Parquet.
summary: DuckDB-Wasm can now open a persistent database directly from the browser's Origin Private File System (OPFS) by passing an `opfs://` path to `db.open`, producing a standard .duckdb file with write-ahead log and checkpoints that survives reloads and browser restarts and opens in the CLI or Python client. This removes the previous requirement to serialize tables to Parquet and stash bytes in IndexedDB at the application layer. The post warns that the current npm `latest` build (1.33.1-dev57.0) silently fails to persist due to a path-canonicalization bug and that users should pin 1.32.0 or use the `next` tag. Because browser tabs seldom close cleanly, it advises calling CHECKPOINT after each batch of writes to guarantee data reaches the main file and to keep reopen fast, with an option to force per-statement checkpoints. Remote Parquet loaded via CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS is cached in OPFS so subsequent loads skip HTTP range requests, and an `opfs: {fileHandling: 'auto'}` option auto-registers opfs:// literals in SQL. The author stresses OPFS is evictable browser storage, not a durability guarantee, and recommends syncing a source of truth to DuckLake or s3:// object storage.
novelty: DuckDB-Wasm now persists via browser OPFS, no manual sync layer
audience: web/devtools engineers building in-browser analytics or offline-first data apps

title: Two-Stack Sliding-Window Aggregation
why: If you maintain a running min, quantile, HyperLogLog cardinality, or even a float sum over a sliding window, this gives you amortized O(1) per push/pop without the error-accumulation bug where a stale NaN or a lost-precision subtraction poisons every future result.
notes: Handles any associative aggregate with no inverse (min/max, quantile, approximate unique count via HyperLogLog, float sum) by abstracting over empty(), unit(x), combine(x,y), finalize(x); Value, Agg, and Out can be three distinct types, e.g. (String, HyperLogLogSketch, u64).

State is two stacks plus one running aggregate: values holds raw elements with values_agg as their aggregate; cum_aggs holds cumulative aggregates of the rest of the window in reverse order. eval combines cum_aggs[-1] with values_agg in constant time.
Amortized O(1) comes from draining values every w-th pop, rebuilding partial cumulative aggregates in O(w); memory is O(w). Window size can grow and shrink dynamically, not just fixed w.

Contrast: the invertible-operator deque trick (add on push, subtract on pop) is simpler but breaks permanently on NaN or infinity and accumulates float error because float addition is not invertible (1e20 + 1 - 1e20 - 1 == -1.0).

Because each aggregate only combines elements currently in the window, outliers poison only the windows containing them and long-term error accumulation is eliminated; Kahan/compensated summation can further reduce per-window float error.

Provenance: author found it in Tangwongsan et al.'s worst-case-constant-time paper, which attributes the two-stack variant to a 2011 Stack Overflow post by 'adamax', itself crediting Sleator's 2001 lecture notes on the two-stack FIFO queue (which does not actually describe windowed aggregation).
summary: The post explains a two-stack algorithm for maintaining an aggregate over a sliding window when the aggregation operator has no inverse, covering cases like minimum, quantile, approximate unique count, and floating-point sum. It abstracts aggregation into empty(), unit(x), combine(x,y), and finalize(x), requiring only that combine be associative, and keeps two stacks (raw values and reversed cumulative aggregates) plus a running aggregate of the values stack. Each eval combines the top cumulative aggregate with the running aggregate in constant time; every w-th pop drains the values stack in O(w) work, giving amortized O(1) per operation and O(w) memory, with support for dynamically varying window size. The author contrasts this with the simple invertible-operator deque approach, which permanently breaks on NaN and accumulates floating-point error because float addition is not truly invertible or associative. A benefit of the two-stack method is that each aggregate depends only on in-window elements, so outliers poison only the windows containing them and long-term error is eliminated, with Kahan summation able to reduce residual per-window error. The author credits the idea to Tangwongsan et al.'s constant-time paper, which traces it to a 2011 Stack Overflow post inspired by Sleator's 2001 two-stack FIFO queue notes.
novelty: simple amortized O(1) two-stack algo for non-invertible sliding-window aggregates
audience: engineers building streaming/stream-processing systems and data pipelines

title: Lambda MicroEgg
why: If you build e-graph rewriting over languages with binders, this shows how to get alpha-equivalent terms to hash-cons identically and capture-avoiding substitution in rewrite RHSes while claiming roughly 3x egg's speed on microbenchmarks.
notes: Built on Max Willsey's microegg; adds built-in unary binders (@sum, @lam), higher-order Miller patterns, and capture-avoiding substitution usable on rewrite right-hand sides. Miller patterns restrict a metavariable to be applied only to distinct bound variables, which the author describes as the decidable core of higher-order matching/unification.

Binder liftings/thinnings are packed into one byte stolen from the u32 Id (a sentinel-1 encoding, credited to AI), so the 'Fat Id' stays 32 bits and first-order terms pay near-zero overhead. The byte caps context at 7 variables; the author floats widening to a 64-bit id or an 'ephemeral enode' side arena for larger thinnings.

Alpha-equivalent terms hash-cons to the same memory, and thinning-related terms share storage: (@lam ... x) and (@lam ... y) nested deeply intern the inner forms identically, which a naive de Bruijn encoding would not. Free variables have an implicit order, so $0+$1 and $1+$0 do not share, but $0+$2 and $0+$1 do.

Self-reported performance: on an AC-10 saturation run (first-order, 262k unions, ~57k e-nodes) match 350ms / apply 1.00s / rebuild 152ms; the higher-order [] variant rises to match 685ms / apply 1.29s / rebuild 151ms. Author compares to egg at ~0.6s for a similar task and estimates roughly 3x egg on microbenchmarks, treating anything under 10x as acceptable; all numbers are self-reported on one machine without methodology.

A separate first-order curried-application form [f x] (HOApp, auto-currying) is offered alongside the usual FOApp; the author notes it costs performance and relates the lambda-free higher-order fragment to superposition provers E-prover and Zipperposition.

Caveats stated by the author: only 'ordered' Miller patterns are supported (metavariable arguments must appear in binder order), which loses power on nonlinear patterns like (foo (lam x (lam y (?a x y))) (lam x (lam y (?a y x)))); the author also says the heavily AI-written Rust code feels 'loose' and that the index-manipulation math was not hand-verified, only tested.
summary: Lambda MicroEgg is a small e-graph tool by Philip Zucker, built on Max Willsey's microegg, that adds well-scoped, alpha-aware binders via a lifting/thinning technique, higher-order Miller patterns, and capture-avoiding substitution in rewrite right-hand sides, driven by an s-expression frontend with a WASM demo. Thinning annotations are stored in a byte stolen from the u32 Id, so alpha-equivalent terms hash-cons to identical memory and thinning-related terms share storage, at the cost of a 7-variable context limit. Miller patterns ({?a x y} notation) constrain metavariables to apply only to distinct bound variables, which the author presents as the decidable fragment of higher-order matching; the implementation further restricts to 'ordered' patterns, trading some expressiveness on nonlinear cases for simpler code. The piece demonstrates sum constant-factoring, map/comp fusion, and object-level beta reduction, and reports AC saturation timings on the order of 1-2 seconds, which the author frames as roughly 3x egg on microbenchmarks (self-reported, single machine, no formal methodology). The author argues the deeper lesson is that contexts, not binders, are the essential concept for giving variable-bearing terms meaning, and discloses heavy AI assistance plus unverified index math, with proofs, wider thinnings, and term-creation in patterns listed as future work.
novelty: e-graphs with scoped alpha-aware binders and Miller patterns
audience: PL researchers and engineers building rewrite systems/compilers using e-graphs

title: AI-Assisted Paper on Z-Library Cites a TorrentFreak Article That Doesn't Exist
why: A peer-reviewed paper from a commercial publisher shipped with fabricated citations that survived editorial review, a concrete example of hallucinated references reaching print with AI named in the acknowledgements.
notes: The paper, 'Z-Library and Full-Text Access: Democratizing Knowledge or Undermining Copyright Ethics?', appeared in New Review of Academic Librarianship (Taylor & Francis) and was written by two librarians at Nigerian universities.

TorrentFreak says at least 10 of the paper's 44 references could not be located, including a nonexistent 2021 TorrentFreak article 'Publishers continue crackdown on shadow libraries' that merely links to the TorrentFreak homepage.

Several citations are misattributed to real scholars: a claimed 2019 Harvard Journal of Law & Technology piece by Daniel Gervais is absent from that issue's table of contents, and a cited Carol Tenopir article does not appear in the named issue; other missing works are credited to Björn Brembs, Smith, Piper, Okike, and Aronson, plus a Kaspersky report.
The acknowledgements state Consensus AI was used to sift literature and ChatGPT was used to improve the language; the authors did not answer follow-up questions about the references.

AI-detection tool Pangram flagged the abstract and conclusion as '100% likely AI-generated'; the article notes such tools produce false positives and that nothing proves AI wrote the fabricated citations.
Taylor & Francis says it referred the matter to its Editorial and Publishing Ethics & Integrity teams; no correction or retraction decision yet.
summary: TorrentFreak reports that a peer-reviewed paper on Z-Library, published this month in Taylor & Francis's New Review of Academic Librarianship, contains fabricated and misattributed citations. The outlet found a reference to a 2021 TorrentFreak article it never published, and could not locate at least 10 of the paper's 44 references, including works falsely credited to IP scholar Daniel Gervais, Carol Tenopir, and Björn Brembs, plus a Kaspersky report. The paper's acknowledgements disclose that Consensus AI was used to sift literature and ChatGPT to improve language, and the AI-detection tool Pangram flagged the abstract and conclusion as likely fully AI-generated, though TorrentFreak notes these tools err and the evidence does not prove AI authored the bad citations. The authors did not answer follow-up questions, and the named scholars did not respond. Taylor & Francis confirmed it referred the case to its editorial ethics and integrity teams and would not comment further during the investigation; whether the paper is corrected or retracted is undecided.
novelty: peer-reviewed journal paper found citing fabricated AI-hallucinated references
audience: researchers, academics, and engineers tracking AI reliability and academic integrity
